children: World Alzheimer’s Day initiative highlights early cognitive changes, timely medical guidance and stronger support for patients and caregivers

Eli Lilly and Company (India) and Fortis Healthcare have called for greater awareness of Alzheimer’s disease and earlier recognition of cognitive changes, as India’s ageing population faces a growing dementia burden. The companies marked World Alzheimer’s Day on 21 September with clinicians and former Miss Universe and actor Lara Dutta, urging families to discuss memory and brain health and seek timely medical guidance.

An estimated 8.8 million Indians aged 60 years and above are living with dementia, according to a nationally representative study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia. The number could reach 16.9 million by 2036 if prevalence remains unchanged, driven largely by the growth of India’s older population.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia and can affect memory, communication, decision-making, independence and everyday functioning. The companies said recognising changes earlier can help individuals and families understand the condition, plan care and access appropriate support.

Doctors also emphasised that Alzheimer’s-related biological changes can begin years before noticeable symptoms emerge. Persistent changes in memory, communication, behaviour or the ability to perform familiar activities can warrant medical evaluation, although memory problems can also have other causes.

Dr Vinit Banga, Director and HOD – Neurology, Fortis Escorts Faridabad, said Alzheimer’s should not be viewed solely through the lens of memory loss. “Alzheimer’s disease is not defined by memory loss alone. It is a complex, progressive neurological disorder in which changes in cognition can gradually affect a person’s ability to communicate, make decisions and function independently,” Banga said.

Dr Sahil Kohli, Additional Director – Neurology, Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Gurugram, said early recognition can help families understand the condition and make informed decisions about care. Lara Dutta, who has spoken publicly about her experience as a caregiver, said conversations around brain health should begin before symptoms are dismissed as normal ageing. “It has made me realise how important it is to pay attention to changes in memory or cognitive health rather than dismissing them as a normal part of ageing,” she said.

Dr Rahul Kapur, Senior Director, Medical, Eli Lilly and Company (India), said addressing Alzheimer’s requires collaboration among healthcare professionals, hospitals, policymakers, patient groups and industry. The initiative sought to encourage a more informed approach to cognitive health and strengthen awareness around timely assessment and support for people living with Alzheimer’s and their caregivers.
